column5: Description

Welcome to the 12th edition of the Letterboxd Season Challenge, hosted by @sethpaul and featuring his original list, where we celebrate 33 exciting new themes ranging across the history of cinema. Started: 9/1/25 Watched: 0/33 Completed: Finished: Ranking 📊 The Letterboxd Season Challenge is a yearly challenge running 33 weeks from September to May (with a 2 week winter break -summer break here in Argentina-). This season will run from September 1st, 2026 through May 3rd, 2027. Each week has a theme, which can be found in the notes of this list, and the goal is to watch and review at least one new-to-you film every week that fits the theme. Once you watch a movie for the Letterboxd Season Challenge, make sure you tag your log with letterboxd season challenge and/or lsc12 along with the weekly tag (e.g. lsc12 week1, lsc12 week2, etc.) so that it is easy for us all to find and read each other's reviews. Although the challenge is organized by week, you are not bound by the weekly schedule and can watch films in any order and as quickly as you want. For many of the themes we've included lists of appropriate films, but you are always welcome to find films on your own as long as they fit the theme. If you happen to watch a different movie that fits a weekly theme, go ahead and log it. If a movie you really wanted to see becomes available, make the swap. Or if you're indecisive or just love a theme, watch multiple films for that week. The important thing is to expand your film knowledge and have fun along the way. The fun starts before the challenge even begins by making your lists! You may create your own or clone this list, but keep in mind that cloning this list won't copy the notes. Here is a document with all the formatting in easily copy-and-pastable form so you can add the notes to your own list. And the discussion continues on the LSC12 Discord, where you can ask questions, get and give recommendations, and talk about anything else film or challenge related. Take a deep dive into LSC12 by visiting LSC12: The Metrics Reloaded to see everything from LSC12's lowest-rated film to how much time the group has spent watching. Now, the most important… Categories and my picks: 1. What Time Is It? - The 4:30 Movie 2. TIFF People's Choice - Brokeback Mountain 3. Ealing Comedies - Kind Hearts and Coronets 4. Nu-Metal - House of Wax 5. As NOT Seen on TV - Mulholland Dr. 6. The Big Question - Enter the Void 7. Sitges Film Festival - Holy Motors 8. British Horror - Eden Lake 9. Whodunit - The Invisible Guest 10. Neo-Expressionism - Ricochet 11. The Wilhelm Scream - The Doors 12. Nowhere to Go - Speed 13. Sex Work - Mysterious Skin 14. Based on a Poem - Onegin 15. Three Wise Men - One Missed Call 16. LB List Battles!: Mommy Issues vs. Daddy Complex - Adoration 17. We Come to This Place for Politics? - JFK 18. Sitting on the Shelf - Collateral 19. Hush Films - Elephant 20. Independent Spirit - sex, lies, and videotape 21. The Feminine Grotesque - Lady Vengeance 22. Grime Time - Suburbia 23. Titles by Saul Bass - Cape Fear 24. Description

Week 1: September 7-13  What Time Is It? It's time to start the clock on the 12th Annual Letterboxd Season Challenge! Our watches don't have to be synchronized, as there are a lot of great options for this week. We initially wanted to make it so the title had to include 12, noon, or midnight, but decided to expand it to any film with a specific time in the title. Whether it's 9:06, High Noon, or 11:11, you can take on the extra challenge of watching the film at the time mentioned in the title. For this week's challenge, watch a film with a specific time mentioned in the title. We've drawn up a list of options to help you save time here. Weekly tag: lsc12 week1

Week 2: September 14-20  TIFF People's Choice Originally called the Toronto Festival of Festivals, the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) turns 50 years old this year. It's one of the most prestigious and largest film festivals open to the public. The public votes on the top prize, the People's Choice Award, which was first awarded to Claudia Weill's Girlfriends in 1978. Since then, the award has frequently gone to films that would later be nominated for, and sometimes win, the Oscar for Best Picture. From 2008-2023, every People's Choice Winner except one was nominated for Best Picture (the only exception was the non-English language film Where Do We Go Now?). The Life of Chuck in 2024 broke the streak and was not nominated, but maybe Hamnet in 2025 began a new streak. Chloé Zhao is the only director to win the award twice. In 2009, the festival introduced separate People's Choice awards for the Documentary and Midnight Madness categories, and while we'd prefer you go for the main competition, we will allow winners from those sections as well. This week's challenge is to watch a film that won the People's Choice Award at TIFF. Weekly tag: lsc12 week2

Week 3: September 21-27  Ealing Comedies Ealing Studios, situated in England, is the oldest continuously-run film and television production company in the world, and they have become well-known for their comedies, but they barely produced comedies during their first few decades of existence, especially during World War II. A few years after the war, Ealing Studios focused on making comedies, and the films produced during these particular eleven years became known as Ealing Comedies. Several of the movies made during this time are considered some of the best British films of all time, and they garnered several BAFTA and Academy Award nominations and wins. These comedies captured a particular post-war spirit of the British people; many of these films feature individuals standing up to social institutions, conventional morality, and rigid notions of class with social commentary that is gentle but still chock full of ironic wit. These films made a star out of Alec Guinness, and a young Peter Sellers found much inspiration from Guinness’ particular brand of comedy featured in these movies. This week, let’s all share a laugh by watching one of the classic Ealing Comedies, which can all be found in this list from MOGGLE89. Weekly tag: lsc12 week3

Week 4: Sept 28-Oct 4  Nu-Metal Korn, Limp Bizkit, Linkin Park. You didn't have to misspell words in your band name to pioneer or popularize nu-metal, but it seems like it helped. Combining heavy metal with hip-hop, grunge, and other genres, nu-metal began in the '90s, with origins tracing back to the '80s, and reached its height in the early 2000s. Filmmakers took notice as well, incorporating the new subgenre into their soundtracks, and the influence extended into many other stylistic choices. Much like the music, these nu-metal films tend to be divisive. Even if they aren't great, they do a great job of transporting you back to this time period. This week's challenge is to watch a nu-metal film. This list and this list are good places to start looking, but this is more based on vibes than any objective classification, so if you find something else that fits, go for it. Weekly tag: lsc12 week4

Week 5: October 5-11  As NOT Seen on TV Remember the old days when movie-watching happened in a theater, and TV shows aired once a week with commercials interspersed throughout their runtime? Back then, American television shows premiered in September and played through till spring, with a summer break. Sound familiar? LSC's unconventional 33-week challenge timeline was predicated on this model, and we've stuck to it, despite the advent of commercial-free streaming services, full-season drops, and anytime-of-the-year-premiere schedules. This week, then, is a throwback of sorts, an homage to a time when television had a more predictable rhythm and format. But, to keep things interesting, we're going to throw a wrench in the works. This week's challenge is to watch a TV pilot for a show that never got picked up. Veteran LSCer MinaGrentham has assembled a gigantic collection of these liminal oddities for you to choose from in her Unsold TV Pilots list. Hey, let's watch some TV! Weekly tag: lsc12 week5

Week 6: October 12-18  The Big Question From heaven to hell and anything in between, no matter what you believe, films have often explored the big question of what happens to us in the afterlife. These films raise fascinating existential questions and range from life-affirming to terrifying. The unknown allows for great creativity. No one can know for sure what the answer is, but while we're all here, we can certainly enjoy and ponder these films. This week's challenge is to watch a film that depicts the afterlife in any form. 𝖘𝖊𝖙𝖍𝖊𝖓𝖘𝖙𝖊𝖎𝖓 has created a list with many examples. Weekly tag: lsc12 week6

Week 7: October 19-25  Sitges Film Festival Although genre films like horrors and fantasies sometimes receive recognition from the most prestigious film awards in the world, it is no secret that they are often overlooked despite their wide appeal, fervent fan bases, and the fact that they often feature powerful performances and innovations in filmmaking. Enter the Sitges Film Festival, which has taken place annually in Sitges, Spain, since 1968 and showcases horror, fantasy, science fiction, and cult films from around the world. Since 1971, they have granted awards called Gorillas to actors and filmmakers, twice giving a Gorilla to the best overall film during its early years, a practice they made regular in 1983. So if you loved Holy Motors or When Evil Lurks, or thought Mia Goth was snubbed for her performance in Pearl, look to the Sitges Film Festival for inspiration for what to watch next. This week, let’s honor genre film by watching a movie that won the Gorilla for Best Feature-Length Film, which can all be found in this helpful list from Cortes Cortes. Weekly tag: lsc12 week7

Week 8: Oct 26-Nov 1  British Horror For Halloween this year, we travel to the country that gave us Hammer Films, Amicus anthologies, and the term Video Nasty. Despite opposition from critics, the UK has produced some of the best (and probably some of the worst) horror films of all time, from gothic ghost stories to folk horror to some truly nasty films. For those who get scared easily, there are plenty of spooky or silly options. Hammer made a series of "mini-Hitchcock" suspense thrillers, and if fast, scary zombies aren't your thing, there are horror comedies like Shaun of the Dead and Anna and the Apocalypse. This week's challenge is to watch a British horror film. Weekly tag: lsc12 week8

Week 9: November 2-8  Whodunit Until recently, whodunits might have seemed like a subgenre on the brink of extinction, but there now seems to be a revival with the likes of Rian Johnson’s Benoit Blanc trilogy and TV shows like Only Murders in the Building and Poker Face becoming popular. It shouldn’t be a surprise, though, because who doesn’t love a good mystery involving a bunch of interesting characters played by some of your favorite actors? A good whodunit invites the audience into the mystery, captivating them with all the possibilities of suspects and motives, to try to uncover the truth alongside the detective or whoever is trying to solve the case. There are other kinds of mystery movies that have continually intrigued audiences, like noirs, serial killer procedurals, and slashers, but whodunits generally seem to be the most fun as they typically involve a large cast of colorful suspects, an eccentric detective, and a surprise reveal at their climax. So grab a magnifying glass, make a chart with all the possible suspects and motives, and play along by watching a whodunit from the list by Stinkeeee here. Weekly tag: lsc12 week9

Week 10: November 9-15  Neo-Expressionism We'll turn it over to user comrade_yui's description from their list:
The rise and fall of analog anti-naturalism: beginning in the late 70s, many films, especially Hollywood genres, began to move away from the focus on verisimilitude and location-shooting that became prominent in the 50s and fully flowered in the early 70s. Neo-expressionism fully became the default style of many famous films from 1983-1996. It faded in the mid-2000s, as greenscreen began to replace sets and lighting in the American cinema began to flatten and resemble television. Tim Burton, Alex Proyas, Russell Mulcahy, early Ridley Scott, and Clive Barker are the masters of neo-expressionism. The essential characteristics of neo-expressionism: /// 1. The embrace of artifice. These are films which no longer pretend to be set in our own world, but instead inhabit a constructed dream-world of sets, matte paintings, and often special effects. /// 2. The post-MTV/commercial hyper-aesthetic. Liquid lighting, wet streets, reflective surfaces, strong monochromatic colors, hard shadows, weather effects, gauze, lens flares, dutch angles. /// 3. Subtextual horror/noir. Many neo-expressionist films are visually oriented in classic horror/noir plots, often featuring monsters, detectives, killers, and assorted goth trappings. Even if the film is not a noir or horror story, it is constructed using the classic visual grammar of those works. /// 4. Decadence. These are films which prioritize a visual experience over narrative cohesion or the minutia of plot, as opposed to the more actorly/scriptural focus of new hollywood films. The actors are here to be in harmony with the overall aesthetic, not to showcase their talents. The scripts are often full of dead-ends. /// 5. Practical effects, first and foremost. Some later neo-expressionist films utilize advances in CGI, but everything is always first grounded in real optical effects, whether that be constructed sets, matte paintings, gels, smoke, stop motion, suitmation, or compositing. The CGI is used to augment the practical effects, never to replace it.
This week's challenge is to watch a neo-expressionist film. Weekly tag: lsc12 week10

Week 11: November 16-22  The Wilhelm Scream Nearly 50(!) years ago, Ben Burtt, sound designer for a little film called Star Wars (oh, you've heard of it?), incorporated a scream (originally from a 1951 Gary Cooper film called Distant Drums) into George Lucas' game-changing, world-altering space opera. In the early 1970s, he and a few other USC film students discovered a studio reel labeled "Man being eaten by alligator" and had been using the stock sound effect in their projects. With the success of Star Wars, that small audio clip spread like wildfire. Throughout the '80s, '90s, 2000s, and beyond, the Wilhelm Scream (named for a character in 1953's The Charge at Feather River, the first film to borrow the scream) found its way into hundreds of movies, a little wink, a little nod, and a little in-joke amongst the sound design community. This week's challenge is to watch a film from Dan Pendleton's Wilhelm Scream list. Have fun, and may the scream be with you! Weekly tag: lsc12 week11

Week 12: November 23-29  Nowhere to Go Being stuck somewhere is a terrifying thought, and filmmakers have used that to their advantage to make horror films, thrillers, survival stories, and surrealist dramas. Characters in these films can find themselves stranded anywhere—a deserted island, atop a tower with no way down, underwater, under the ground, on a bed, or at a dinner party. Will they find a way out or be trapped forever? That simple question will provide enough drama for any film you choose. This week's challenge is to watch a film from the Getting Stuck in Terrible Places Cinematic Universe. Weekly tag: lsc12 week12

Week 13: Nov. 30-Dec. 6  Sex Work Since the very first days of film, the movies have embraced sex. Attitudes over the last 130-odd years have, however, changed, waxing and waning, most notably with Hollywood's implementation of the Hays Code in the mid-1930s (they're not married!?) and the social progressiveness of mid-1960s and '70s America (mainstream pornos!?). Throughout this time, a subset of sex on film has quietly but continually carved a niche for itself: sex work. In much the same way as society's tolerance levels, sex work on film has changed, too. Up until recently, depictions of sex work (and workers) on film tended to skew towards the stereotypical, depicting their characters as glamorized fantasies, simple victims, or even mere machine gun fodder doomed to violent punishment. Fortunately, things have evolved. The mere fact that we have the term "sex worker" in place of traditional labels such as "prostitute" or "hooker" shows that attitudes—and understanding—are, once again, shifting. So, too, do recent entries in the canon. Films like Anora and The Menu are joining rare, earlier gems like Working Girls to prove that filmmakers can and should depict sex workers with complexity, agency, and nuance, while avoiding the tropes that historically pigeonhole these characters and their stories. Whether you aim for an earlier example that proves problematic or opt for something more recent that may reject caricatures, your challenge this week is to watch a film from sex worker and Letterboxd member Krissy Victory💋's Sex Worker🫦💕💋❤️💰✨ list. Weekly tag: lsc12 week13

Week 14: December 7-13  Based on a Poem Of course, it makes complete sense that there are a multitude of movies based on novels. It even makes sense that there are some full-length features based on short stories; their film adaptations simply expand the narrative and thematic content. Curiously, however, there are also a handful of movies based on poems. The most obvious movie adaptations of poems are of narrative and/or epic poems, which don’t always even require expansion like Beowulf; however, the best film adaptations of poems adapt the mood and tone that the language implies through visual and sonic means, no matter how distinct of a narrative the poem contains. This week, watch a movie that is uniquely based on a poem. Here is a helpful list from DRMIII. Extra points for also reading the poem the movie was based on. Weekly tag: lsc12 week14

Week 15: December 14-20  Three Wise Men Christmas is almost upon us, which means the three wise men are on their journey to bring gifts, this time in the form of movies. The first is Frederick Wiseman, who brings the gift of documentaries about American Insitutions. The second is Robert Wise, who brings the gift of films spanning almost every genre you can think of. The third is Ray Wise, who brings the gift of an extensive filmography that includes Twin Peaks, Swamp Thing, and RoboCop. This week's challenge is to watch a film by or starring one of these three "Wise" men. Weekly tag: lsc12 week15

Week 16: January 4-10  LB List Battles!: Mommy Issues vs. Daddy Complex Ladies and Gentlemen, tonight, for your entertainment, we are proud to present the return of LB List Battles in conjunction with the World Psychoanalytic Complex Championship! Now, turn your eyes to the center ring as we introduce the fighters: In the XY corner, the challenger, hailing from the minds of Freud and Jung, Daddyyyyyyyyy commmmmm-plexxxx! And in the XX corner, the reigning champion, whose roots reach all the way back to Greek mythology, Mommyyyyyy issuessssss! Never before has a more perfect battle of psychological conditions been pitted against each other! Tonight, you'll bear witness to unconscious associations and unwitting impulses stemming from unhealthy parental relationships developed in childhood and manifested, in all their messy glory, under the bright lights of this storied venue! Now, let the battle begin! This week's challenge is to take it to the generational ropes and do emotional battle by choosing a movie from fallenangel's Mommy Issues list or ☘️caitlín☘️'s Lolita | Nymphet | Age Gap | Daddy Issues list. And may the most malignant disorder... prevail? Weekly tag: lsc12 week16

Week 17: January 11-17  We Come to This Place for Politics? Although escapism is a valid and essential aspect of engaging with movies, so too is engaging with them as works of art that have something important to convey, even politically. When the New Republic reached out to film critics, programmers, and academics in 2023 for their opinions on the most significant political films, one declined by stating, “Every film I care about is political.” As true as this statement may be about most movies as movies reflect humanity, some films are more overtly political than others by centering on elections, demonstrations, strikes, coups, revolutions, wars, and genocides or by centering on political issues like racism or feminism. Filmmakers like Oliver Stone, Spike Lee, Sergei Eisenstein, Jean-Luc Godard, Leni Riefenstahl, Raoul Peck, and Jia Zhangke are well-recognized for their political films. This week, engage politically with a film by watching one of the top 100 movies selected by the 79 respondents to the New Republic’s question for the most politically significant films, which are compiled by GoodScreamer in this list here. Weekly tag: lsc12 week17

Week 18: January 18-24  Sitting on the Shelf For many of us, collecting physical media is just as much fun as watching the films. Rather than spend hours scrolling through streaming options, why not just grab something from the shelf that you already know you're interested in seeing? If you're like us, you probably own several films that you bought blindly and haven't made time for yet. This is the week to fix that. This week's challenge is to watch a film that you own physically but haven't seen yet. If you don't own any physical media, that's ok. You can either check out a DVD from your local library, or feel free to "borrow" something you haven't seen from Wade's shelf and watch it in whatever format you can. Weekly tag: lsc12 week18

Week 19: January 25-31  Hush Films Shhh. Ever since The Jazz Singer paired image with sound (synchronized recorded dialogue, to be precise), people have been vociferously yammering in the movies. And you know what? Sometimes, it's nice to take a break, maybe queue up a restrained film, something that quietly entertains you, the picture of serenity and calm. All nice and well, we say, but what if we take it a step further? Instead of mere tranquility and restraint, what if we go FULL HUSH? Let's turn the volume knob on Nigel Tufnel's amp (the one that goes to eleven) to zero. Let's adhere to the first rule of Fight Club and not talk about it. Let's buck the new-fangled modern trend and seek something with minimal to no dialogue. Let's hush. This week's challenge is to shut your (and everyone else's) trap and watch a film from Letterboxd list-maker extraordinaire ꪖꪶꪑꪖ's 🤐 NO WORDS 🙊 list. And if anyone asks what you're doing, bring your index finger to your lips and hit 'em with the shush gesture: it's hush films week! Weekly tag: lsc12 week19

Week 20: February 1-7  Independent Spirit The Independent Spirit Awards were first held in 1986 to honor the 1985 film year and have continually sought to champion films that don’t have big studio financial backing. Films considered for awards must now have a $30 million or under budget, which has increased over the years due to increasing production costs. Before 1994, the sole requirement was based on financial criteria, including a percentage of funding that had to come from independent sources, whereas now, movies that are backed by a studio can still be eligible for consideration if the subject matter of the film is deemed original and/or provocative. Uniqueness of vision, innovation, and diversity are also considered. A secret committee selects the nominations so they cannot be influenced by the filmmakers in any way, and the voting for the winners is conducted by all Film Independent Members, an organization anyone can join for a fee. The Best Feature award was first awarded to Martin Scorsese’s After Hours, and over the years, there has been an increase in overlap with winners of the Oscars’ Best Picture award. This week, get into the spirit of indie films by watching a movie that won Best Feature at the Independent Spirit Awards. Here is a list of those movies compiled by Brian, who has participated for many years in LSC! Weekly tag: lsc12 week20

Week 21: February 8-14  The Feminine Grotesque The madwoman in movies has always intrigued audiences, especially in the 1940s when Bette Davis reigned supreme and in horror movies where the scale may tip in favor of suggesting we should hate or fear feminine madness instead of developing any understanding of it. Film critic Angelica Jade Bastién created the term feminine grotesque to describe the dark side of womanhood, female madness, and extreme emotion that can complicate female strength, desire, beauty, and autonomy. As Bastién defines it herself:
The emotional, social and psychological problems that are specifically connected to the character’s sense of womanhood provide the meat and gristle of this genre. . . . Like women’s pictures, The Feminine Grotesque offers visual liberation from the confining strictures of the patriarchy. No matter how temporary, women are able to see themselves as bold, defiant, vulnerable, sexually realized, ambitious and hopeful. The films of The Feminine Grotesque obsess over female desire and subjectivity, but even with this strong feminist impulse, the genre is often muddled by endings that show these women integrating themselves but lacking any hope for a future. In cinema, like in life, it often feels like there is rarely hope for the madwoman.
This week, investigate the way female madness is depicted by watching one of Angelica Jade Bastién’s Feminine Grotesque movies from her list here. Weekly tag: lsc12 week21

Week 22: February 15-21  Grime Time Feel like gettin' grimy? Good. There's no better way to scratch that itch than with moviedom's most wide-ranging and deviant subgenre, EX•PLOI•TA•TION! Consider just a few of the boundless varieties exemplified in that one word: blaxploitation, sexploitation, Ozsploitation, and nazisploitation. Don't care for the -sploitation suffix? Maybe pinku, cannibal, women in prison, or mockbusters are more your thing. Sure, we've highlighted a few of the sub-subgenres in past LSCs, such as beach party, kaiju, luchador, peplum, and giallo, but there's just so much more out there! Maybe LSC will stick around long enough to dedicate a week to every conceivable option, but we wouldn't bet on it, and what's more, who wants to wait until LSC77 to find an excuse to finally catch up with one of the hundreds of thought-provoking, not-at-all-derivative sharksploitation movies swimming around on your favorite free streaming service? Not us! So, here's the deal: let's plunge our fingers into the exploitation swamp and yank a title from the putrid muck that is Andrew Liverod's The Exploitation List - or how I learned to stop worrying and love the sleaze. Thankfully, Andrew has done a lot of the hard work for us, selecting five representative titles from each of a cornucopia of exploitation subgenres. The only thing you have to do is decide which sort of grime will fill your time! Weekly tag: lsc12 week22

Week 23: February 22-28  Titles by Saul Bass Saul Bass is arguably the most famous title designer in cinematic history. He invented kinetic typography, which is when words move across the screen or appear to fly in from off-screen, which is still in popular use today. He first became famous within the film industry for his title sequence for The Man With the Golden Arm, which incorporated the themes and tone of the movie into its design, which usually wasn’t done, and thoroughly impressed audiences. After this success, Bass was hired by many prominent directors, including Alfred Hitchcock, for several of his most famous movies, not only to design and produce title sequences, but to design posters and other live-action sequences in the movies as well. Bass worked with Elaine Makatura on the title design sequence for Spartacus, and they ended up getting married and working to design title sequences for the rest of their lives. From the mid-60s to the late-80s, the Basses moved away from title design to focus on raising their children and directing their own short films and one full-length feature, especially as many directors were opting to design their own title sequences anyway. Being such big fans, James L. Brooks and Martin Scorsese convinced the Basses to return to title sequence design, which the Basses worked on together until Saul Bass died in 1996. This week, bask in the artistic genius that was Saul Bass by watching a movie he designed the title sequence for, which can all be found here. Weekly tag: lsc12 week23

Week 24: March 1-7  Rumberas Rumberas was a genre of film popular during the Golden Age of Mexican cinema in the 1940s and 50s, named after their star dancers of the rumbera, Afro-Caribbean rhythms or Cuban rumbas, a dance-style that was eventually taken over by the mambo and cha-cha-chá. These dancing heroines were often involved in plots that saw them forced into prostitution despite humble and good-natured beginnings, who still deserved punishment for their “sin,” although later films depicted them as low-class women willing to “sin” for money, while jungle rumberas depicted an entirely primitive and amoral universe where sin wasn’t even a concept. These movies made stars out of several of their leads, many of them Cuban, at a time when female actors rarely achieved star status in Mexico. This genre died out very quickly in the mid-50s as the movies all started to seem the same, and as the Mexican government began cracking down on cabarets and nightlife. This week, explore this extinct and unique genre from Mexico by watching a rumberas film. This list from Joshua Minsoo Kim can help. Weekly tag: lsc12 week24

Week 25: March 8-14  Genie in a Moosehead Lager Bottle It's nearly Oscar time! Let's forget about that award-giving juggernaut for a minute and focus our attention northward, to the land of snow, hockey, maple syrup, and a whole lot more, Canada. Since 1949, the Canucks have been handing out film awards. Their version of the Oscars has morphed over the years, changing names and formats. However, the mission has remained the same: to highlight the best films that The Great White North and its endlessly creative, uniquely visionary inhabitants have to offer. This week, rub a Moosehead Lager bottle to summon a title from this list, which compiles all the nominees from 1980 to 2012, when the awards were called the Genies. Weekly tag: lsc12 week25

Week 26: March 15-21  Best of the Least Seen In early 2026, Letterboxd switched from an Official Top 250 Films to 500 Films. Along with this update, a required minimum of 25,000 ratings was required to be eligible for the list, up from 15,000. This increase is, in part, due to the growing popularity of Letterboxd, but also to mitigate how quickly new movies can land on this top list. As a result, several films dropped off the list for not having enough ratings. There is an Official List, curated by Sam Williams, that lists the Top 100 Underseen Films, which contains the highest-rated movies that fall beneath the 25,000 ratings threshold, but still have at least 1,000 ratings. In other words, these are the movies most likely to become part of the Top 500 Films once enough people have seen them. Many users have asked Sam if he will increase the list from 100 Underseen Films since the Official List doubled in size, but Sam maintains that 100 is a good threshold for featuring movies that actually could one day make the Top 500 list due to their extremely high ratings. So far, 31 films from this list have “graduated” to the Top 500 list. Let’s see if we can help one of these movies graduate to the Official Top 500 list and watch an underseen gem from Sam Williams’ Top 100 Underseen Films. Weekly tag: lsc12 week26

Week 27: March 22-28  Contemporary Performers: Léa Seydoux It is no small feat to break into Hollywood as a foreign actor and still oscillate so seamlessly between big blockbusters and smaller arthouse fare, but Léa Seydoux has done so with great aplomb, often appearing in several films a year. Her breakout role was in 2008’s A Beautiful Person, which helped land her small roles in Hollywood movies like Inglorious Basterds, Midnight in Paris, and Mission Impossible: Ghost Protocol, but it was 2013’s Blue Is the Warmest Color that cemented her stardom and she’s now done just about everything from appearing in several Wes Anderson movies to being a Bond girl. Still, her best roles are as leads in international films, like France or The Beast. Seydoux has truly worked with many great directors in a wide variety of movies. As Yasmin Omar wrote:
You never know what you're going to get when you sit down to watch a Léa Seydoux film. She could be a tattoo-sleeved pothead, a sexually reawakened widow or a gun-toting assassin. She could be a misbehaving nun, a mentally unstable news anchor or a disfigured performance artist.
So this week, choose your Seydoux, whether that be her role in a popular blockbuster or, as we recommend, one of her powerhouse performances as a complex lead, all of which you can find here. Weekly tag: lsc12 week27

Week 28: Mar 29-Apr 4  Cannes Grand Prix We typically include a week covering the winners of a prize from one of the big film festivals. We've done all of the top prizes, at least the most famous ones, so for this week we're focusing on the Cannes Grand Prix. Despite the name, which seems like it should be the highest honor, it is given to the runner-up. Many times we'll watch one of these and wonder how the Jury didn't give it the Palme d'Or, and other times we wonder why it won anything at all. More often than not, though, these are great and unique films that are absolutely worth seeing. Andrei Tarkovsky, Bruno Dumont, Nuri Bilge Ceylan, and Matteo Garrone have all won the award twice. This week's challenge is to watch a film that won the Cannes Grand Prix. Weekly tag: lsc12 week28

Week 29: April 5-11  The Art of Fight Choreography When it comes to cinematic artistry, certain elements tend to crowd the mind: cinematography, score, costuming, and maybe even production design. But anyone who has seen a Bruce Lee or contemporary wuxia film can certainly grasp the artistry of modern fight choreography. Early films, on the other hand, featured simplistic skirmishes, their fight sequences typically a means to an end rather than delivering any value in and of themselves. But in the 1970s, that all changed. Thanks to Hong Kong studios like Shaw Brothers and Golden Harvest, fight choreography—rooted in martial arts—became a crucial part of storytelling and another powerful tool in a filmmaker's tool chest. Meanwhile, the American film industry took some time to catch on, reluctantly shedding its age-old basic stage combat and tentatively carving out a narrow niche for a certain generation of action stars. Eventually, the rest of Hollywood came to understand screen combat's value, and these days, you'd be hard-pressed to find a fight sequence in any film worth its salt that didn't employ a fight choreographer as a true artist, par excellence. This week's challenge is to strap on a harness, hook up to a wire, and soar gracefully through Jack🧠's The Art of Fight Choreography list. Land a decisive blow by choosing a film, and don't forget to thank your fight choreographer for making it all look so effortless! Weekly tag: lsc12 week29

Week 31: April 19-25  Coffee & Donuts To the extent that there could ever be a sure-fire formula for a successful movie, the buddy cop flick makes a compelling specimen. You're probably familiar with it, but here's what that recipe typically looks like: take one aging vet and one hotshot newbie with disparate personalities, force them together in pursuit of a common goal, and watch the fireworks! Quarreling gradually gives way to respect and then friendship, all slathered in pure entertainment achieved through action, comedy, bromance, and the added cherry on top of good triumphing over evil. And while not every movie in the subgenre faithfully adheres to the winning formula concocted in Walter Hill's seminal 48 Hrs., they don't dare deviate too much. This week, grab a fried dough ring and some dark bean water (if you feel like embracing the stereotype) and settle in with a title from Todd Gaines's Coffee & Donuts: A Beginner's Guide To Buddy Cop Movies list. And, hey, watch it with a partner! Weekly tag: lsc12 week31

Week 32: Apr 26-May 2  Classic Performers: Errol Flynn The quintessential swashbuckling hero, Errol Flynn is best known for playing perhaps the best version of Robin Hood. He frequently collaborated with the great Olivia de Havilland on screen and a lot of other women off-screen. Looking into his life, even for a classic Hollywood movie star, we were surprised by the many scandals of his hedonistic lifestyle. He died from a heart attack at the age of 50, after appearing in 66 films. This week's challenge is to watch a film starring Errol Flynn. Weekly tag: lsc12 week32

Week 33: May 3-9  The Long and Short of It --𝘔𝘰𝘮𝘮𝘺, 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘥𝘰 𝘮𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮? Making a feature-length film is a big undertaking. So, for those without the requisite funding, industry connections, or name recognition, short films are the most logical way to birth a movie. A short film is cheap. A short film is brief. A short film is a precious idea packed into a mini package, easily presentable, digestible, and (hopefully!) marketable. However, not every short film grows into a feature-length film. Some are just perfect as they are, a Goldilocks concept in a Goldilocks runtime. But others are a springboard, an opportunity to whet the appetite of an angel, borne on cinematic wings, to convey a cherished vision to full actualization. Now, not every blossoming of a short film is advisable. Some, for whatever reason, make an uninspiring transition. However, others fill out quite nicely, as if life had begun in a mature state. But, no, we know their secret: --𝘚𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦𝘴, 𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘵𝘭𝘦 𝘰𝘯𝘦, 𝘮𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘳𝘵 𝘧𝘪𝘭𝘮𝘴. This week's challenge is to wrap up another LSC with not one, but two films from 𝖘𝖊𝖙𝖍𝖊𝖓𝖘𝖙𝖊𝖎𝖓's The Long and Short of It list. Choose a short (or feature) and its progeny (or forebear) and witness the miracle of movie birth! Weekly tag: lsc12 week33
